opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question. If I wrote a book on hybrid simulators, I'd want it to be the book I wish I'd had as a first-year PhD student, when I was trying to understand why methods like PIC, FLIP, APIC, and MPM actually work.

I'd start with the core tension in physical simulation: Eulerian versus Lagrangian views. Eulerian grids are great for things like pressure projection, incompressibility, and computing derivatives. Lagrangian particles are great for tracking material, handling advection without much numerical dissipation, and carrying history like deformation. Hybrid methods try to get the best of both by passing information back and forth between particles and a background grid. So the first part would build intuition for why you'd want that marriage at all.

Then I'd go through the transfers very carefully: particle-to-grid and grid-to-particle. Most of the subtle problems live there. PIC is very dissipative, FLIP is noisy, and APIC and the affine and polynomial variants fix a lot of that by preserving angular momentum and carrying more local velocity information. I'd want to explain these with clear derivations, but also with pictures and small runnable examples, so readers can see the dissipation or the noise with their own eyes.

The middle of the book would be the Material Point Method, since it's the most general framework in this family. You can do snow, sand, foam, mud, elastic solids, and fracture in one framework. I'd cover constitutive models, plasticity, return mapping, and also practical things like MLS-MPM, which simplifies the implementation a lot. Being able to write an MPM solver in about 88 lines of code always felt meaningful to me, because it shows these methods don't have to be intimidating.

I'd also want a strong performance-engineering section, because in practice hybrid simulators are memory-bound and full of scattered writes. You run into sparse data structures, particle sorting, atomics on GPUs, and load balancing. That's a big part of why I built Taichi. The algorithm on paper and the fast implementation are very different things, and most textbooks don't bridge that gap.

Finally, I'd look at newer directions: differentiable simulation for control, inverse design, and learning; coupling between solids and fluids; and how these simulators connect to robotics and machine learning.

Overall, I'd want the book to combine rigorous math, physical intuition, and real code. Ideally a reader would finish it able not just to understand a SIGGRAPH paper, but to implement it and make it fast.

r001.rationale: The response mentions differentiable simulation for learning and connections to machine learning, but does not clearly propose covering how simulation and neural networks are integrated.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a fun question, because I've actually thought about this a lot. The field of hybrid simulation, meaning mixing different representations like particles and grids, or Lagrangian and Eulerian views, has grown up a bit scattered. You learn MPM from one set of papers, FLIP and PIC from another, SPH from yet another, and nobody really connects the dots.

So the first thing I'd want to cover is the "why." Why do we hybridize at all? Pure particle methods are great at tracking material and handling topology changes, but computing derivatives on scattered points is painful. Pure grid methods give you nice, stable differential operators, but you get numerical dissipation and you lose track of where material actually is. Once people see that each representation is good at one thing and bad at another, the whole design space of hybrid methods becomes obvious. You're just choosing which quantities live where.

Then I'd go through the methods as variations on a theme rather than as separate things. PIC, FLIP, APIC, PolyPIC, MPM, they're all the same transfer loop with different choices about what information you carry back and forth. If you present them that way, the reader can invent their own variants, which to me is the real goal.

A big chunk would have to be about implementation, because that's where most people actually get stuck. Data layouts, sparse grids, how to make the particle-to-grid scatter not become a bottleneck, how to get it to run on a GPU. I would want the book to have real, runnable code, probably in something like Taichi, so every chapter ends with something you can execute and modify in a few dozen lines. I think a book on simulation without working code is kind of dishonest.

And then I'd want a chapter on failure modes. Grid-crossing instability, ringing, volume loss, the places where the theory is clean but the simulation explodes. Those are the things you only learn by suffering through them, and I'd love to save people that suffering.

If I could include one more thing, it'd be differentiability. Once your simulator is written in a clean, hybrid way, making it differentiable is natural, and that opens up control, inverse problems, and learning. I think that's where the field is going, so the book should end there.

r001.rationale: The candidate proposes a chapter on differentiability and mentions learning, but does not describe integrating simulation with neural networks.

astra-6.text:
I’d want to start with what we mean by a hybrid simulator—what we’re combining, and why. For example, you might use a physics-based model for the parts you understand well, and a learned model for the parts that are difficult or expensive to compute. The interesting question is how to make those pieces work together reliably.

Then I’d build up practical examples, covering the tradeoffs between accuracy, speed, and stability. I’d also want to discuss how you validate the result: when does the hybrid approach actually help, and when is a simpler simulator a better choice? Ideally, readers would come away able to build one themselves and understand its limitations.

r001.rationale: The response proposes combining a physics-based model with a learned model, but it does not identify neural networks as part of the integration.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d want to start with what we mean by a hybrid simulator, because that can mean several things. You might combine particles and grids, or combine a traditional physics solver with a learned component. The interesting question is why you choose each representation and how you make them work together.

Then I’d build up some concrete examples, explain the numerical methods, and show how to implement them efficiently. I’d also want to cover the failure cases—stability, conservation, and what happens at the interface between different methods. Ideally, readers would come away with enough intuition to design their own simulator, rather than just reproduce an example.

r001.rationale: The response mentions combining a traditional physics solver with a learned component, but it does not identify neural networks as the component or clearly propose covering their integration.
